title: Say who said it (Avot 6:6)
hookLine: quoting in the name of the one who said it brings redemption, as Esther did
tomorrow: a whole book of Talmud, start to finish. where do you even begin?

cards: A friend says something brilliant at lunch. Two days later you post it, word for word, and it gets more likes than anything you've ever written. Nobody asks where it came from.
So whose line is it now? The last of Avot's forty-eight ways answers that, and it attaches a surprisingly big promise.

teach.h: SAY IT IN THE NAME OF WHO SAID IT.
teach.b: Avot says: whoever says a thing in the name of the one who said it brings redemption into the world. The proof comes from the book of Esther. Mordecai overhears two guards plotting to kill the king.

teach.h: ESTHER TELLS IT IN MORDECAI'S NAME.
teach.b: He tells Esther, and Esther tells the king, in Mordecai's name. Why would credit bring redemption? Two readings live in the tradition, and they pull different ways.
The first follows the plot. Because Esther named Mordecai, his deed was written in the king's book of chronicles.
Later, on a sleepless night, the king has that book read to him, finds Mordecai's name, and honors him, and the story turns toward rescue.

teach.h: READING ONE: CREDIT IS A SEED.
teach.b: On this reading, credit is a seed: a name written down at the right moment changes what happens next. The second reading follows the speaker.

teach.h: READING TWO: THE LIPS STILL MOVE.
teach.b: The Talmud says that when a teaching is repeated in a sage's name in this world, his lips move in the grave. On this reading, credit isn't about outcomes at all.
It keeps a person in the conversation, still speaking after they're gone. One reading looks at what credit does for the future. The other, at what it owes the past.

Here's one to tell a friend tonight: the Talmud's tractate of blessings, where this path goes tomorrow, says things like, Rabbi Avin bar Rav Ada said in the name of Rabbi Yitzchak. Two names, so neither one goes quiet.

how: In Jewish study it's customary to cite a teaching with its chain of names, 'so-and-so said in the name of so-and-so', and many teachers credit even a student's insight by name.

games.q: what does “say who said it” mean?
o: introduce yourself by name before you speak in class
speak the name of God aloud before you begin to learn
repeat a teaching in the name of the one who said it

games.q: the saying and its two readings — tap the pairs.
p: overhears the plot against the king
tells the king in Mordecai's name
credit is a seed for what comes next

s: in Avot, naming your source is just good manners
Avot says it brings redemption into the world, and proves it from the book of Esther.
Esther told the king about the plot in Mordecai's name
and that credit was written in the king's book of chronicles.
later, a sleepless king finds Mordecai's name in his book
he has the chronicles read to him, finds the deed, and honors Mordecai.

games.q: you lean toward reading one: credit matters because of what it sets in motion. now give reading two its best case.
o: naming a teacher keeps them speaking; credit is owed to the past, whatever it changes.
naming a teacher protects you if the quote later turns out to be wrong.
naming a teacher makes your own point sound more important to others.
games.why: reading two doesn't need a happy ending: when a teaching is said in a sage's name, the Talmud says, his lips move in the grave. the debt is to the speaker.

practice: Think of one line you repeat as your own: a phrase, a kitchen trick, a piece of advice. Trace it back to whoever first said it to you, and say their name out loud, once, along with the line.
Then keep them in mind for the rest of the sit.

wordCard.voice: Say who said it. The last of Avot's forty-eight ways: repeat a teaching in the name of the one who said it.

orig.note: Hebrew: whoever says a thing in the name of the one who said it.

carryVoice: For the road: say who said it, and the name keeps speaking. That's Avot, finished.

sources.ref: Mishnah Avot 6:6 (whoever says a thing in the name of the one who said it brings redemption into the world)
Esther 2:21–23; 6:1–3 (the plot told in Mordecai's name; written in the chronicles; the sleepless king)
Babylonian Talmud, Yevamot 97a (a sage's lips move in the grave when a teaching is said in his name)
Babylonian Talmud, Megillah 15a; Berakhot 6a (the saying with the Esther proof; 'Rabbi Avin bar Rav Ada said in the name of Rabbi Yitzchak')
